item.title: 'An affront to historical justice': China strongly condemns Japan's negative moves related to notorious Yasukuni Shrine
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-17 22:16:00
China strongly condemns Japan’s latest negative moves related to the notorious Yasukuni Shrine, a spokesperson for the Chinese Embassy in Japan said on Saturday, warning that Japanese politicians’ actions reveal their true intention to cover up Japan’s wartime crimes, distort historical facts and pave the way for accelerating remilitarization. The spokesperson made the remarks in response to a question about the Japanese leader making ritual offerings to the war shrine and certain cabinet members and lawmakers visiting the shrine. During WWII, Japan launched the war of aggression and committed horrendous crimes. The so-called Yasukuni war shrine is a spiritual tool and symbol of Japanese militarism. It honors 14 convicted Class-A war criminals directly responsible for the war of aggression, the spokesperson noted. The spokesperson stressed that no pretext whatsoever can hide the Japanese politicians’ true intention to change the verdict on the war criminals, cover up Japan’s war crimes, distort the historical facts, and pave the way for accelerating remilitarization. “The relevant erroneous actions are an affront to historical justice, a challenge to the foundational norms of civilization, and a provocation against the postwar international order,” the spokesperson said, adding that such behaviors have been firmly rejected by the international community. Noting that this year marks the 80th anniversary of the opening of the Tokyo Trials, the spokesperson said that to view and treat history correctly is an important prerequisite for Japan’s postwar return to the international community, the political foundation for Japan’s ties with neighboring countries, and, more importantly, a key measure of Japan’s commitment to peaceful development. The spokesperson solemnly urged the Japanese side to seriously reflect on its history of aggression, face up to its war crimes, exercise prudence in words and deeds on issues related to the Yasukuni war shrine, and make a clean break with militarism. Japan should earn trust from its Asian neighbors and the rest of the world with concrete actions, the spokesperson said. Global Times

item.title: Canton Fair stories spanning generations show China's leap from selling products to offering innovative solutions
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-17 19:35:00
Global buyers watch and film a China-made robot playing badminton at the 140th Canton Fair in Guangzhou, South China's Guangdong Province, on October 15, 2026. Photo: VCG At the first phase of the 140th China Import and Export Fair, commonly known as the Canton Fair, a crowd gathered around a booth. Inside, a humanoid robot plays badminton - it swings, returns, and smashes while layers of buyers press in with phones held high. Outside the crowd, Michael Lee Chi-fung, deputy general manager of the Hong Kong trading firm Yuen Tai, paused. His mind turned to his grandfather Lee Fuen. In the spring of 1957, Lee Fuen boarded a coal-fired train from Hong Kong to Guangzhou for the very first Canton Fair - China's flagship trade exhibition, still held twice a year to connect Chinese manufacturers with global buyers. The star attractions at that edition were 100,000 lovebirds and 10,000 golden-coin turtles, sold alongside silk and Foshan paper umbrellas from Guangdong. At that edition, total turnover reached $17.54 million; agricultural products and handicrafts made up more than 60 percent. A total of 1,223 buyers from 19 countries and regions walked into the exhibition hall of just 9,600 square meters. Global buyers at the exhibition hall for industrial products at the first edition of Canton Fair in Guangzhou, South China's Guangdong Province, on April 25, 1957. Photo: Courtesy of Canton Fair Lee Fuen went on to attend 126 consecutive sessions without missing one. He visited factories, improved packaging, and helped introduce brands such as Tsingtao Beer to Hong Kong's market and beyond. His grandson Michael Lee has now attended nearly 50 sessions himself. "My grandfather's generation did the zero-to-one," Michael Lee told the Global Times. "They made sure China had something to sell." That was the era of "having something to sell." The Canton Fair was a window the country pushed open; outsiders looked in to see what China could offer. In the decades that followed came the "one-to-ten" phase. Canned goods and silk gave way to home appliances, machinery and equipment. By the 86th session in 1999, mechanical and electrical products had become China's largest export category for the first time. Talip Murat Kolbaşi, chairman of Arzum, Turkey's leading home-appliance brand, has attended more than 60 sessions. He remembered the questions of buyers changing from "Can the price be lower?" to "Can you make it to our standard?" "Most of our company's most innovative and best-selling products have their origins at the Canton Fair. We hope to use the platform to explore international markets further," Kolbaşi said. "Similar projects elsewhere can take a long time. In China, the speed from concept to reality far exceeds expectations." Kenneth Ng, managing director of Sanyu Industrial (Holdings) Co, first came to the Canton Fair as a child in 1968 with his father. He became a buyer in his own right in 1985, at the age of 20. "Many products are now automated and intelligent," he told the Global Times. "In textiles, you put in the raw material and the machine does the rest. Machines run 24 hours; if a thread breaks, they find and fix the problem themselves. Before, a broken thread stopped everything. AI helps a great deal. When my father brought me into this hall, I could never have imagined today's level of sophistication - or that an entire exhibition hall would struggle to hold all the robot companies." Phase One of the 140th session is a vivid example of the third chapter of China's trade. Under the theme "Advanced Manufacturing," more than 12,000 companies are attending, with 17 dedicated zones for emerging and future industries forming a complete chain from core components and intermediate goods to finished machines. The number of first-time releases of service robots, smart medical devices and drones rose by about 20 percent. A manager at Shandong Tools Manufacturing Co put the change simply: "Customers used to ask about price first. Now they ask about quality, technology and complete solutions." Gao Jianhua, vice general manager of Tsann Kuen (Zhangzhou) Enterprise Co, described another kind of upgrade. The long-standing small-appliance exhibitor has moved from pure OEM (making products to other companies' designs) to ODM (designing and manufacturing under its own intellectual property). "In the past, most of our work was OEM - the customer's design, the customer's appearance. Now, for automatic coffee machines, steak grills, food-preparation equipment and smart garment care, many of the designs and patents are ours. We cooperate with foreign clients in ODM form. That is a big adjustment," Gao said, adding that 126 foreign buyers had confirmed they would visit its booth before the session even opened. The shift came in stages. In recent years, the company has invested more heavily in its own design capability. "We used to chase volume. Our grill series once held more than half the global market. Now we go deeper into quality, convenience and intelligence," said Gao. Eric Ong Lim, president of Mindanao Rock in the Philippines, did not linger in the exhibition hall on October 16, the second day of the session. He went straight to the Foshan factory of exhibitor Foshan Namkoo New Energy Technology Co to inspect the production line and discuss deeper cooperation. What buyers now want is no longer a single machine but a package of capabilities, Yuan Feng, sales director at Namkoo, told the Global Times. After the factory visit, Lim's assessment was clear: "The product quality is very good. I'm very satisfied and much more confident to invest than before." Wu Changhua, chairman and president of Must Energy (Guangdong) Tech Co., Ltd, told the Global Times that "during the day, buyers look at products at our booth at the Canton Fair; at night they come to our factory in Foshan to talk about deeper cooperation." Guangzhou-based industrial IoT platform provider iROOTECH offers another illustration of the shift toward "selling capability." The company serves more than 120 countries and over 1,100 large clients worldwide. "Our direction is helping our customers build AI-powered factories of the future, using agents to guide production robots," Xu Zinan, sales director at iROOTECH, told the Global Times. As many exhibitors at the Canton Fair put it: The question the world asks is no longer only what China sells, but whom it is helping to build - and how well.

item.title: Paraguay tech minister's response to China's countermeasures a deliberate attempt to shift responsibility
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-17 16:28:00
Illustration: Liu Xiangya/GT Days after China announced countermeasures against Paraguay's Minister of Information and Communication Technologies Gustavo Emigdio Villate Samaniego over his wrong moves on the Taiwan question, he wrote lengthy posts on social media, which Chinese experts describe as an attempt to shift responsibility by framing the move over his own misconduct as targeting the entire country. In a post on his X account, Villate called the countermeasures “a certification that what we have been doing since 2023 is the correct path.” He also declared that Paraguay's relationship with the Taiwan region would "never be on the table as a bargaining chip." His remarks may sound defiant, but they turn cause and effect on their head: They recast interference in China's internal affairs as "sovereign diplomacy," and portray collusion with separatist forces as "cooperation between two democracies." Here is why China took the countermeasures against Villate and Belize Minister of Foreign Affairs and Foreign Trade Francis Fonseca. In announcing the measures, a spokesperson for the Chinese Foreign Ministry pointed out that certain politicians in Paraguay and Belize willingly serve as chess pieces for Taiwan's Democratic Progressive Party (DPP) authorities in their pursuit of independence by soliciting external support. "Their visits to Taiwan and reception of 'Taiwan independence' separatist forces in their countries constitute severe interference in China's internal affairs. They also attacked and smeared China by spreading the 'Chinese cyberattack' disinformation, causing egregious impact in the world," the spokesperson said. Apparently, the word that apparently struck a nerve with Villate was chess piece, or "pawn" as he puts it in his social media post. Villate’s decision to speak out loudly several days after the countermeasures were announced was an attempt to salvage his credibility after being exposed for his collusion with “Taiwan independence” separatist forces, Xin Qiang, director of the Taiwan Studies Center at Fudan University, told the Global Times on Monday, adding that Villate is putting on a stunt for people in Paraguay and DPP authorities to gain support. Villate seeks to turn China’s countermeasures against him into a political narrative about Paraguay "defending its right." Yet his refusal to reflect on his erroneous actions, and his determination to "accelerate" them, only further reinforce the impression that he is acting as a “pawn.” Villate also sought to frame his attempt to pursue certain so-called technology cooperation projects with DPP authorities as being in the interest of Paraguay, despite what experts describe as limited benefits and enormous costs in various fields. “Villate wants to convince people that his actions will bring prosperity to Paraguay, but there is no such thing as a free lunch,” Zhang Wensheng, deputy dean and a professor at the Taiwan Research Institute at Xiamen University, told the Global Times, adding that the move actually puts Paraguay's national interests and its people's welfare at risk. For years, voices within Paraguay's agricultural sector have called for reconsidering the country's diplomatic policy, hoping to gain access to China's market for beef, soybeans and other products. For a developing country seeking to expand agricultural exports, attract investment and upgrade its industries, the absence of normal diplomatic relations with one of the world's largest economies creates tangible obstacles. There is one thing Villate gets right: Beijing's message "deserves careful reading." Unfortunately, he has read it entirely backward. Being the only country in South America that still maintains so-called diplomatic relations with the Taiwan authorities is hardly a badge to boast about. Rather, it highlights how far Paraguay has moved against the prevailing international trend. More troublingly, the erroneous actions of certain politicians like Villate will also be borne by the country and its people. Ordinary people across the world want to pursue better lives through good jobs and development rather than by interfering in other countries’ internal affairs. Binding one's future to "Taiwan independence" separatist forces is not a path toward greater autonomy. It is a dead end that risks forfeiting development opportunities and leaving a country increasingly isolated internationally. The author is a reporter with the Global Times. opinion@globaltimes.com.cn

item.title: 'Bold creativity', but 'certification remains crucial': Chinese auto industry leaders react to Tesla's 'flying car' Roadster
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-17 14:15:00
A photo of the Roadster Photo: Tesla US tech giant Tesla held an event at a SpaceX rocket test site on Thursday US time and officially unveiled its second-generation Roadster, which has been widely described as a "flying car," drawing considerable attention from China, with many Chinese auto industry leaders commending the innovation. Notably, the car is also open for reservations in China, though actual delivery plans remain unclear. Video footage of the demonstration has been widely shared on Chinese social media, and many also turned their attention to how Chinese auto executives view the "flying" Roadster. Li Bin, Chinese electric vehicle (EV) maker NIO's founder, chairman and CEO, reposted a link to Tesla's demonstration video of Roadster on Sina Weibo and commented: "This is incredible! We really don't have this - thumbs up for Tesla." The comment appears to be a nod to a previous remark made by Li. The NIO founder once declared that "whatever Tesla has, I have; and what I have, Tesla doesn't." Now, as Tesla's Roadster sparks heated discussion, Li's remarks from eight years ago have been dug up again and quickly become a viral internet meme, according to some auto industry news outlets. He Xiaopeng, chairman of EV maker XPENG, said in a post on WeChat that the Roadster represents "a very cool alternative form of a flying car," according to several media reports. He added that whether the product can be realized depends on flight safety, performance parameters, range, and crucially, flight certification. He noted that these requirements require long-term efforts both in China and the US and expressed hope that progress can accelerate. Zhao Deli, founder of XPENG AEROHT (ARIDGE), the flying car affiliate of XPENG and the first company in China to mass-produce a flying car, said the demonstration showcased "bold creativity" and vector-control technology. "This helps more people believe in the future of flying cars," said Zhao. In a livestream of the demonstration on Thursday local time, Tesla demonstrated additional capabilities. The Roadster slowly followed a C-shaped suspended track, hovered while oriented vertically relative to the ground, and remained suspended at the top parallel surface of the track. After accelerating off the upper end of the track, the vehicle adjusted the direction of its thrusters mid-air to perform a 180-degree flip before landing smoothly. According to Tesla's official website, the Roadster is offered in three versions - Performance, Thrust and Rocket. All three are listed with an estimated range of approximately 300 miles (483 kilometers) and a top speed exceeding 230 mph (370 kilometers per hour). In the US, reservations are open for the Performance version with a deposit of $50,000 and the Thrust version with a deposit of $250,000. The Rocket version is available by invitation only. Tesla's China website currently accepts reservations only for the Performance version, with a fully refundable deposit of 332,000 yuan ($49,653). The site notes that whether the vehicle can ultimately be sold in a given market will depend on applicable local laws and regulations at the time of launch. Tesla CEO Elon Musk stated that production of the Roadster is scheduled to begin in 2028. According to previous reports, the original Roadster was first delivered in 2008 at a price of about $100,000 and was discontinued in 2012. Tesla announced plans for a new Roadster in 2017 with a target delivery date of 2020, but the project has faced repeated delays. Global Times

item.title: Apple's iPhone Duo pre-orders sell out in seconds in China, with some deliveries delayed until next year
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-17 14:03:00
An Apple store in Beijing Photo: VCG Apple's first foldable phone, the iPhone Duo, priced starting at nearly 16,000 yuan ($2,391) in China, did little to dampen the enthusiasm of Apple fans rushing to buy it. Pre-orders opened at 8 pm on Friday, and the initial allocation quickly sold out. The strong demand underscores the enormous potential and robust purchasing power of China's consumer market, a Chinese expert said. As of press time on Saturday, Apple's official website showed an expected delivery date of January 22, 2027. On Chinese e-commerce platform JD.com, all models in the iPhone Duo series were out of stock, and on Apple's official flagship store on Tmall, an estimated delivery window had been pushed back to January 23, 2027. Meanwhile, the rapid sellout of the initial stock has driven up the "scalper prices" for the iPhone Duo. Global Times asked several sellers on Chinese secondhand trading platform Xianyu and found that the markup on the first batch of iPhone Duo stock is generally over 4,000 yuan. A veteran Apple fan surnamed Tao told the Global Times that he grabbed one on his phone last night, buying the most expensive 2TB version. He said that it was extremely popular on Taobao at the time and sold out in an instant; he succeeded in placing an order on the Apple Store app only after refreshing it repeatedly. At the time of ordering, it showed delivery in early November, but after the order was confirmed, the estimated shipping time was pushed back by a week - roughly November 14 to 21, Tao said. The iPhone Duo, Apple's first flip phone, is on display at one of the company's product launch events on September 9, 2026 Photo: VCG Notably, on Tmall, although the iPhone Duo was not yet available, many consumers had already begun purchasing accessories such as iPhone Duo phone cases. A top-selling iPhone Duo phone case was priced at 192 yuan and showed more than 300 units sold. The strong pre-order demand shows that Chinese consumers still have a strong appetite for high-quality products, and the Chinese consumer market still has enormous potential and tremendous purchasing power, Li Changan, a professor at the Academy of China Open Economy Studies at the University of International Business and Economics, told the Global Times on Saturday. TF International Securities analyst Ming-Chi Kuo noted in an industry survey that assembly shipments of the foldable iPhone in the second half of 2026 will be 7 million to 8 million units, of which third-quarter shipments will be between 500,000 and 1 million units, according to financial news outlet 21jingji.com. The frenzy over the iPhone Duo coincides with Tim Cook's China visit. As executive chairperson of Apple Inc, Cook kicked off the trip on October 11 with an arrival in Guangzhou, capital of South China's Guangdong Province. This marks his first China tour since stepping down as CEO on September 1. In a meeting with Chinese Commerce Minister Wang Wentao on Thursday, Cook said that Apple is optimistic about China's development prospects, will further expand its business in China, and is willing to play an active role in promoting the stable and sound development of US-China economic and trade relations, according to the Ministry of Commerce.

item.title: Kindergarten head sentenced to life imprisonment for adding toxic substances to food served to children, staff
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-16 22:27:00
Heshi Peixin Kindergarten in Maiji district, Tianshui, Northwest China's Gansu Province Photo: CCTV A Chinese court on Friday sentenced the head of a kindergarten in Northwest China’s Gansu Province to life imprisonment for instructing staff to add toxic and harmful non-food substances to meals served to children and employees, while five other defendants received prison terms ranging from six to 15 years. The kindergarten’s principal Li Huifang was sentenced to life imprisonment, deprived of political rights for life, and ordered to forfeit 500,000 yuan ($70,000) in personal assets. Zhu Jinglin was sentenced to 15 years in prison and fined 300,000 yuan. Four kitchen staff members at the kindergarten – Niu Aiyuan, Wen Yafang, He Xuxia and An Chunling – received prison terms ranging from six to eight years and were also fined. The court found that Li, the de facto person in charge of the Heshi Peixin Kindergarten in Maiji district, Tianshui, and Zhu, the kindergarten’s executive director, violated national food safety regulations by instructing and arranging for the four kitchen workers to add toxic and harmful non-food substances to food prepared and served to children and staff, causing serious consequences. Six people were arrested in 2025 after deliberately adding toxic lead-containing pigments to children's food, which poisoned 247 pre-schoolers, a government investigation reported on Sunday, according to the Xinhua News Agency in July 2025. The kindergarten principal directed the practice to make food appear more colorful and attractive for marketing, Xinhua reported. The investigation, ordered by Gansu's provincial leadership and involving state environmental and health experts, concluded that cooks at the Heshi Peixin Kindergarten added pigments clearly labeled "inedible" into flour to make corn rolls and date cakes. These pastries have been served to children and staff on a monthly basis since May 2024. Of the kindergarten's 251 children tested, 247 had abnormal blood lead levels (including 14 additional cases identified during follow-up testing), as well as 28 staff members, per Xinhua. Global Times

item.title: No bullying the small, no blackmail by the small: China's South China Sea rule
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-16 18:11:00
Philippines South China Sea Illustration: Liu Xidan/Global Times Recent remarks by Chinese Ambassador Jing Quan have been portrayed in Manila as a threat. In fact, they restate a consistent Chinese position: firm defense of territorial sovereignty and maritime rights, together with a preference for peace, restraint and managing differences through direct dialogue. In the South China Sea, China will not use its size to bully the small, nor allow the Philippines to use its smallness to blackmail the strong. China’s approach to territorial and maritime disputes has remained stable for decades. It safeguards its territorial sovereignty and maritime rights while consistently advocating peaceful settlement through bilateral negotiation and consultation. This principle applies not only to the South China Sea but also to other territorial and maritime questions involving its neighbors. The disputes between China and the Philippines have a long history. China maintains that they stem primarily from the Philippines’ occupation of eight features in China’s Nansha Islands beginning in the 1970s and its subsequent claim over Huangyan Island. Overlapping maritime claims also emerged as the international law of the sea developed. Successive Philippine administrations have repeatedly taken actions that have aggravated tensions, including arrests of fishermen from the Chinese mainland and Taiwan, and the unilateral initiation of the South China Sea arbitration case, which China opposed as contrary to prior bilateral understandings and the principle of state consent. China regards its responses to infringement and provocation as legitimate measures to defend its rights. The equality of states under the United Nations Charter and general international law does not give any country a free hand to manufacture incidents at sea. Where a state has illegally occupied another state’s territory, the latter retains, in principle, the right of self-defense. China has exercised considerable restraint, prioritizing regional stability and preserving space for dialogue. That restraint should not be mistaken for the absence of limits. The disparity in national strength, particularly maritime capabilities, between China and the Philippines is an objective fact. Manila cannot expect its repeated provocations, public smearing, and the suspension of military communication channels to be met indefinitely with silence. China has treated the Philippines as an equal neighbor, but restraint is not unlimited. Effective management of maritime differences depends substantially on whether the Philippine government can restrain its military and coast guard. Persistent difficulties in bilateral relations serve neither country’s interests and are particularly damaging to the Philippines’ development. Regional countries should jointly safeguard the region’s hard-won peace and development. Whenever the two sides have moved toward dialogue, certain forces within the Philippines, particularly its military and coast guard, have manufactured incidents to disrupt progress. These forces appear driven less by public welfare than by external powers’ preferences and their own political or institutional interests. If Manila calls for dialogue while allowing these forces to create friction and stoke anti-China sentiment, bilateral communication mechanisms will struggle to function. China and the Philippines are permanent neighbors. Maritime disputes do not change this geographic reality. External military equipment and joint military exercises cannot reverse the regional balance of power. Nor can repeated invocations of a “China threat” narrative resolve the Philippines’ domestic development challenges. Manila may believe that militarization and maritime incidents demonstrate its value as a “frontline platform” for the US and other Western countries, securing stronger security guarantees and economic benefits. Such expectations overlook external powers’ independent strategic calculations. External powers may provide equipment and diplomatic backing while using the Philippines’ geographic location to strengthen their military posture. Their support does not guarantee a willingness to bear the costs of escalation. If a crisis spirals out of control, distant powers can reduce their involvement, leaving the Philippines to face the consequences. History offers repeated warnings about tying national security to another country’s strategic agenda. Manila should weigh that risk carefully. China-Philippines relations stand at a crossroads. Continued tolerance of maritime provocations will invite bolder moves and further damage bilateral ties. The immediate priority for the Marcos government should be to restrain adventurist impulses within its military and coast guard, halt provocations and information operations directed against China, and return to bilateral dialogue and consultation. Only sustained dialogue, supported by restraint and consistent action, can manage differences and stabilize ties. The author is director of the Research Center for International and Regional Studies at the National Institute for South China Sea Studies. opinion@globaltimes.com.cn

item.title: Chinese navy hospital ship arrives in Cote d'Ivoire on medical mission
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-16 10:56:00
Local honor guards welcome the Chinese People's Liberation Army Navy hospital ship Auspicious Ark upon its arrival in Abidjan, Cote d'Ivoire, Oct. 14, 2026. Auspicious Ark arrived in Abidjan, the economic capital of Cote d'Ivoire, on Wednesday to begin a friendly visit and provide medical services, marking the first visit by a Chinese naval hospital ship to the country. The hospital ship, which is carrying out Mission Harmony-2026, docked at Abidjan at about 10:00 a.m. local time (1000 GMT). (Photo by Yvan Sonh/Xinhua) The Chinese People's Liberation Army Navy hospital ship Auspicious Ark arrived in Abidjan, the economic capital of Cote d'Ivoire, on Wednesday to begin a friendly visit and provide medical services, marking the first visit by a Chinese naval hospital ship to the country. The hospital ship, which is carrying out Mission Harmony-2026, docked at Abidjan at about 10:00 a.m. local time (1000 GMT). Ivorian military and government officials, China's ambassador to Cote d'Ivoire, the defense attache and embassy staff, as well as representatives of the Chinese community and Chinese enterprises welcomed the ship at the port. On board, Chinese naval personnel and civilian staff stood in formation and waved to the welcoming crowd at the port. At the welcoming ceremony, local residents held banners and waved the national flags of China and Cote d'Ivoire to welcome the Chinese naval hospital ship. After the ceremony, the Chief of Staff of the Ivorian Navy boarded the Auspicious Ark and toured the hospital ship. During the seven-day visit, the hospital ship will provide medical treatment for local patients aboard the vessel, while medical personnel will visit the Abidjan Military Hospital and a local university, among other places, for medical exchanges and medical services. The mission will also organize a deck reception to strengthen friendship and mutual trust with the Ivorian side. item.title: 'Forced labor' in Xinjiang's salmon industry, too? The New York Times has lost it: Global Times editorial
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-15 23:44:00
A salmon farm in Nilka County, Ili Kazak Autonomous Prefecture, Xinjiang Uygur Autonomous Region. Photo: VCG In their attacks on Xinjiang-related issues, some Western media outlets are still deliberately presenting themselves as "objective and fair," but the signs of preconceived bias and a narrative assembled to fit a predetermined agenda are all too clear. Ultimately, no amount of smearing by US media can erase Xinjiang's economic and social development, nor can it stop people of all ethnic groups at the foot of the Tianshan Mountains from striving for a better life. Recently, The New York Times published a purported in-depth investigative report about the fish farming industry. The article adopts the posture of a "neutral" investigation, citing global research and evidence from multiple sources. It ranges from Peruvian fishing vessels and fishmeal processing plants to offshore aquaculture pens in Norway. Yet in the second half of the article, the focus takes a sharp turn toward the salmon industry in Northwest China's Xinjiang, devoting extensive coverage to recycling familiar allegations such as "forced labor." Read closely, the report reveals a familiar pattern: In their attacks on Xinjiang-related issues, some Western media outlets are still deliberately presenting themselves as "objective and fair," but the signs of preconceived bias and a narrative assembled to fit a predetermined agenda are all too clear. The report offers no evidence from firsthand interviews to support its claims about Xinjiang. Instead, it pieced together much of its narrative from vague attributions with phrases such as "claim," "accuse," and "most likely." By using documented problems in the seafood industry in other parts of the world to shape readers' perceptions in the first half, the article encourages them to assume that the claims made in the second half are equally well substantiated. However, the report provides no solid evidence that similar problems exist in Xinjiang, while packaging subjective speculation as so-called "investigative findings." Such journalistic practices run directly counter to the most basic standards of media credibility. Why are US media outlets willing to lose their credibility just to push out similar fake reports? The real aim, it would appear, is to lend support to Washington's unilateral sanctions targeting Xinjiang. From cotton and tomatoes to sunflower seeds and dumplings, and from solar photovoltaics to polysilicon, the pattern remains the same, with the focus now shifting to Xinjiang's cold-water fish industry: Any competitive industry that benefits Xinjiang's local communities is targeted with the "human rights" cudgel, as negative media coverage is paired with unilateral sanctions to suppress Chinese competitive industries and contain development in China's western regions. It's important to point out that what these sanctions are really aimed at is the employment and development rights of people of all ethnic groups in Xinjiang. In fact, Xinjiang's salmon industry is a prime example of how local resources can be harnessed to turn geographical disadvantages into drivers of development. It is also a tangible achievement of China's campaign to develop its western regions in the new era. Nilka County in the Ili Kazakh Autonomous Prefecture benefits from glacial meltwater flowing down from the Tianshan Mountains. The water remains cold and rich in dissolved oxygen throughout the year, and its excellent quality provides exceptional natural conditions for cold-water fish farming. Technologies such as automated feeding, underwater cleaning robots, and semi-closed recirculating aquaculture systems help minimize pollution, while uneaten feed and fish waste can be processed into organic fertilizer. The farming process emphasizes raising fish without medication and at low stocking densities. Companies in the industry have also obtained multiple international food safety certifications. Their products serve the domestic market and are exported to countries across Southeast Asia, the Middle East, and Europe. They have even gained access to Singapore, a market known for its stringent food standards. Turning desert landscapes into productive fisheries and snow-capped mountains into a source of premium seafood is an industrial success achieved through Chinese ingenuity and hard work. The benefits to people's livelihoods, brought about by industrial development, are being tangibly enjoyed by the people of all ethnic groups. Under a model that combines leading enterprises, employment in industrial parks and social security, some farming and herding families whose livelihoods have revolved around pastoralism for generations have moved into companies and become industrial workers, earning stable wages. Some herders also receive dividends through equity investments. Many young people have chosen to return to their hometowns for work closer to home. The salmon industry has also spurred the growth of fish-themed agritourism, specialty restaurants, rural tourism, and related businesses, opening up additional sources of income and giving fresh impetus to rural vitalization. These concrete, visible improvements in people's lives stand in stark contrast to the falsehoods propagated by some Western media outlets. Ultimately, no amount of smearing by US media can erase Xinjiang's economic and social development, nor can it stop people of all ethnic groups at the foot of the Tianshan Mountains from striving for a better life. It is hoped that some Western media outlets that pride themselves on being "fair and objective" will drop their self-deceptive tactics and go to Xinjiang to see the real production scenes for themselves, listen to workers on the ground describe their own experiences, and gain a firsthand understanding of what human rights really mean to the people of all ethnic groups in Xinjiang - and what rights they genuinely enjoy and deserve to have respected.

item.title: OpenAI CFO's claim of cybersecurity risks about Chinese AI models driven by business interests amid open-weight competition: expert
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-15 20:18:00
OpenAI CFO Sarah Friar speaks at the at the International AI Summit in Dublin, Ireland, on October 14, 2026. Photo: VCG OpenAI Chief Financial Officer (CFO) Sarah Friar reportedly warned businesses using Chinese artificial intelligence (AI) models to consider what she called safety and security elements, while claiming that companies should favor Western models for cybersecurity-related applications. A Chinese AI expert told the Global Times that the security of AI models cannot simply be judged by where their developers are based, nor by labeling them as "Chinese" or "Western." More relevant factors include deployment, data isolation, access permissions and security management. There is insufficient technical basis or evidence to assume Western models are inherently safer than Chinese ones, the expert said, adding that Friar's remarks also reflect the pressure major Western AI companies are facing as Chinese models become increasingly competitive in cost, deployment and real-world applications. Speaking at the International AI Summit in Dublin on Wednesday, Friar claimed companies embracing Chinese models should consider the "safety and security elements," adding that "we think you want to be on more Western models on the cyber front," according to Bloomberg on Wednesday. The Bloomberg report also said OpenAI and Anthropic are under pressure from advances among open-weight AI models. Friar's claims come as Chinese open-weight models are gaining influence in the global developer ecosystem. A report published by AI platform Hugging Face in August said several Chinese labs had moved rapidly toward the frontier of open models in 2026. The report said that "In almost every month of 2026, the largest and most performant open model from a Chinese lab was larger than any model an American lab released." The downloads of Alibaba's Qwen's broader release strategy across model sizes reached 2 billion. Qwen-based models now account for 151,448 derivatives on the platform, according to the report. OpenAI itself has a history of publicly releasing research and model technology. When the organization was established in 2015, it said researchers would be strongly encouraged to publish papers, blog posts and code. In 2019, OpenAI released the full 1.5-billion-parameter GPT-2 model together with its code and model weights. Per its website, OpenAI also currently offers gpt-oss open-weight models. Xiang Ligang, director-general of the Zhongguancun Modern Information Consumer Application Industry Technology Alliance, told the Global Times on Thursday that companies often open up technology early on to attract developers, expand ecosystems and improve their models, but commercial priorities grow as AI moves toward large-scale applications from earlier stages of research and training. "OpenAI's shift from emphasizing openness to protecting market interests reflects this change," Xiang said. However, using security concerns to discredit competitors without clear technical evidence could also prompt users elsewhere to question whether their models are inherently safer, the expert added. OpenAI's own models have also been involved in significant security incidents. The company disclosed that during internal cybersecurity evaluations in July 2026, its models circumvented controls designed to isolate them from the internet and compromised parts of OpenAI's internal research infrastructure and Hugging Face's systems. Australian officials separately disclosed in September that an OpenAI AI agent had gained unauthorized access to an Australian public website during model training in June. Officials identified the incident as "very serious," even though no personal information was accessed during that incident, according to a readout of the press conference. The security claim from OpenAI also comes as the company is looking to cybersecurity as a potential source of future growth. The Irish Times reported on Wednesday from the same Dublin summit that cybersecurity, life sciences and drug development could become future growth drivers for the company. Friar said AI companies should be "selling solutions" in areas such as cybersecurity rather than "selling fear," while arguing that AI could help identify vulnerabilities in older code and patch them at "machine speed." Commercial competition is "undoubtedly" a factor, Xiang pointed out. As OpenAI's CFO, Friar's remarks cannot be separated from the company's business interests and market competition, he said. Xiang added that as Chinese open-weight models gain ground with advantages in cost and practical deployment, OpenAI is under growing pressure amid growing competitions to turn its AI capabilities into sustainable revenue, including through areas such as cybersecurity. In this context, security risk claims over Chinese models also serve to protect its commercial interests.
